questions.stem: What does 'bail out' mean in: 'The government bailed out the failing bank.'?

options.option_text: To criticise harshly (wrong context for 'bail out')
To rescue from financial difficulty (correct: bail out = provide emergency financial help to prevent collapse ✓)
To completely abandon (wrong: 'bail on someone' = abandon; 'bail out' = rescue)
To investigate thoroughly (wrong context)

questions.explanation: B is correct. BAIL OUT (transitive) = to rescue someone or an organization from financial trouble by providing money. 'The government bailed out the failing bank' = provided emergency funds to prevent the bank from collapsing. Also used: 'bail out of' (intransitive) = to escape from a dangerous situation.

questions.stem: Choose the correct meaning of 'run out of': 'We've run out of time.'

options.option_text: To race against time (wrong — 'running against time' is a different phrase)
To have no more of something (correct: run out of = exhaust the supply of something; 'no time remaining' ✓)
To escape from a time limit (wrong — 'run out' doesn't mean escape from something)
To calculate the remaining time (wrong context)

questions.explanation: B is correct. RUN OUT OF = to use up/exhaust a supply of something so that none is left. 'Run out of time' = have no time left. 'Run out of money' = have no money. 'Run out of ideas' = have no more ideas. Very common phrasal verb in both everyday and exam English.

questions.stem: 'She couldn't ______ the news of her friend's death.' Choose the correct phrasal verb.

options.option_text: get over (correct: get over = recover emotionally from something difficult ✓)
get through (get through = manage to survive a difficult period or contact someone successfully — slightly different meaning)
get away (get away = escape from a place or situation)
get by (get by = manage with limited resources or minimum needed)

questions.explanation: A is correct. GET OVER = to recover from something emotionally or physically. 'She couldn't get over the news' = she couldn't emotionally recover from the shocking news. Compare: get through (survive a difficult period), get away (escape), get by (manage financially or otherwise). The 'GET' phrasal verb family is very frequently tested.

questions.stem: Choose the correct phrasal verb: 'The factory ______ 500 units of the product every day.'

options.option_text: turns off (turn off = switch off an electrical device; wrong context)
turns out (correct: turn out = produce; 'the factory turns out 500 units' ✓)
turns down (turn down = reduce volume or reject an offer; wrong context)
turns over (turn over = flip, or in business = generate revenue; less natural here)

questions.explanation: B is correct. TURN OUT (among many meanings): (1) to produce — 'the factory turns out 500 units'; (2) to happen/result — 'how did things turn out?'; (3) to attend an event — 'a large crowd turned out.' In manufacturing context, 'turns out' = produces.

questions.stem: What does 'look into' mean in: 'The police will look into the complaint.'?

options.option_text: To physically examine the inside of something (literal meaning — wrong in this context)
To investigate or examine a matter (correct: look into = investigate or inquire about something ✓)
To ignore or overlook (wrong — 'look into' is active investigation, not ignoring)
To resolve or settle (look into = investigate, not necessarily resolve)

questions.explanation: B is correct. LOOK INTO = to investigate or examine a matter carefully. 'The police will look into the complaint' = investigate the complaint. Compare: look after (take care of), look up (search for information), look out (be careful), look down on (regard as inferior), look forward to (anticipate with pleasure).

questions.stem: Choose the correct phrasal verb: 'He ______ as the new manager while the original was on leave.'

options.option_text: stood in (correct: stand in = temporarily take someone's place/role; 'stood in as manager' ✓)
stood out (stand out = be noticeably different or better than others)
stood up (stand up = rise from sitting; also = fail to keep an appointment)
stood by (stand by = support someone; or remain available; not 'temporarily replace')

questions.explanation: A is correct. STAND IN (for someone) = to take someone's place temporarily. 'He stood in as manager' = temporarily acted as manager. STAND OUT = be conspicuous. STAND UP = rise or fail to keep an appointment. STAND BY = support/be ready. These STAND- phrasal verbs are frequently tested.

questions.stem: What does 'account for' mean in: 'Exports account for 30% of the country's GDP.'?

options.option_text: To explain the reason for (one meaning of 'account for' — but the sentence is about proportion)
To constitute or represent a proportion (correct: in this context, 'account for' = constitute/represent ✓)
To be held responsible for (another meaning of account for — but not used in proportion context)
To calculate exactly (wrong — 'account for' doesn't mean to calculate)

questions.explanation: B is correct. ACCOUNT FOR has multiple meanings: (1) To constitute/represent a proportion — 'Exports ACCOUNT FOR 30% of GDP.' (2) To explain — 'How do you account for this error?' (3) To be responsible for — 'He must account for his actions.' In the sentence, 'account for' = represent/constitute 30% of GDP.

questions.stem: 'The charity event ______ over ₹50 lakhs for the flood victims.' Choose the phrasal verb.

options.option_text: gave up (give up = stop trying/doing something; wrong context)
raised up (wrong: 'raise money' is standard; 'raised up' is not the correct phrasal form for money)
raked in (correct: rake in = earn or accumulate a large amount of money ✓)
ran up (run up = accumulate a debt; wrong connotation for charity fundraising)

questions.explanation: C is correct. RAKE IN = to earn or accumulate money (often in large amounts). 'The charity event raked in ₹50 lakhs' = collected/earned ₹50 lakhs. 'Give up' = stop; 'Raised up' is not standard; 'Run up' = to accumulate (usually debt). Also acceptable: 'collected', 'raised' (single verbs), but 'raked in' is the phrasal verb option here.

questions.stem: What does 'see off' mean in: 'Her family went to the airport to see her off.'?

options.option_text: To defeat someone easily (wrong meaning of 'see off' in competitive contexts)
To accompany someone to their point of departure as a farewell gesture (correct ✓)
To take someone to the hospital (wrong context)
To observe someone from a distance (wrong — 'see off' is an active farewell)

questions.explanation: B is correct. SEE OFF = to accompany someone to their point of departure (airport, station, bus stop) as a farewell. 'Her family went to the airport to see her off' = to say goodbye at the airport. In sports context, 'see off' = to defeat or eliminate a competitor (different meaning). Context is crucial.

questions.stem: Choose the correct phrasal verb: 'He ______ a new business plan and presented it to the board.'

options.option_text: drew on (draw on = to use something as a resource — 'drawing on experience')
drew up (correct: draw up = to prepare or write a formal document or plan ✓)
drew out (draw out = to extend/prolong — 'draw out a meeting')
drew off (draw off = to remove a liquid; wrong context)

questions.explanation: B is correct. DRAW UP = to prepare a formal document, plan, contract, or list in writing. 'Drew up a business plan' = prepared/formulated a business plan. Compare: DRAW ON (use as resource), DRAW OUT (prolong, or elicit information), DRAW UP also means (pull up, stop a vehicle). 'Drew up a contract/will/list/plan' — all standard uses.
